cases.body: 第一步是按原文版本固定环境和数据修订：IndicDiarBench的Hugging Face修订、PyTorch 2.1.1、pyannote.audio 3.1.1的DiariZen代码库提交、scikit-learn和NumPy版本，以及父模型权重和声纹模型的许可。注意许可分开：基准CC BY 4.0，父分割权重CC BY-NC 4.0只允许非商业研究，对手系统各按自有条款，商用接口与可下载权重是两回事。推理按16秒窗、1.6秒步长、最大概率加11帧中值滤波、无重叠帧提向量、凝聚初始化后VBx的流程跑，关闭TF32、固定种子、每文件重置以保证确定性。补充材料称包含分数文件和重画图表脚本，可先从分数文件复算池化和时长加权，再重跑推理核对按字节一致。口径实验只需在输出后桥接同说话人间隙，不要重训网络。容易误解的是把事后桥接的下降当成系统提升，它只是测量口径的灵敏度分析。

draft.readerTitle: 印度二十二种语言里谁在何时说话：Anuvani-Diarization 的零样本适配与标注口径分析
draft.oneSentenceThesis: 论文在全部22种印度 scheduled 语言的1164段录音上零样本比较九个说话人日志系统，用印度电话银标签适配分割网络得到时长加权16.78%的错误率，并证明话语内停顿是否切分这一标注口径能带来1.9到4.1个百分点的系统性差异。

conceptBridges.explanation: 说话人日志指输入一段多人会话音频，输出每个时刻谁在说话的时间线；日志错误率是把漏检语音、虚警语音和说话人混淆三段时间加总后除以参考语音总时长，越低越好，它把有没有声和是谁的声音放在同一把尺子上衡量，因此后文讨论停顿切分会直接影响漏检和虚警的划分。
端到端分割指神经网络在短窗内直接逐帧判断当前有哪几个局部说话人在发声，天然能处理重叠；向量聚类指把每个局部说话人的纯净帧做成声纹向量，再跨窗口聚成全局说话人，二者搭配是因为前者只管局部谁在响，后者解决跨越长时间后同一人前后对应，组合后才能处理任意时长和任意人数的录音。
幂集分类是把四个局部说话人所有可能的同时发声子集编码成16个互斥类别，每帧只选一类；重叠指同一时刻不止一人在说话，传统一次只给一人的做法无法表示它，用幂集后重叠只是其中一类输出，模型在16秒窗内最多区分四个同时说话的局部身份，更多全局人数靠后续聚类展开。
WavLM编码器是自监督预训练的语音特征提取器，负责把16kHz波形变成能区分音色和内容的帧表示；Conformer头是堆在编码器之上的四个同时看局部卷积和全局自注意力的块，负责把特征变成每20毫秒一类的分割判决，适配时两者参数一起微调，是因为印度会话的信道和口音同时改变了底层声学和局部轮转模式。
话语级标注指转写员按一句话一段来切分，话语内部几百毫秒的停顿不切断；词对齐标注指按强制对齐把边界放在声学停顿处，话语内停顿会被切开，前者适合按说话人归属整理文字，后者适合做声学分析，同一套声学判决在两种口径下漏检和虚警会反向变化，所以不存在一种切分能同时在两种基准上最优。

sections.heading: 说话人日志要回答什么，输入输出和必须保留的信息是什么
sections.body:
说话人日志的输入是一段单声道会话音频，时长从几分钟到几十分钟不等，里面有两到九个说话人，可能混用语言、互相打断、同时说话，还可能经过电话、近场麦克风、远场会议麦或网络视频等不同信道。目标是输出一条时间线：每个时刻谁在说话，允许同一时刻标出多人重叠。必须保留的信息有两层，一是有没有人声，二是这段人声属于全局的哪一个说话人编号。评价时用日志错误率同时惩罚三类时间：该标没标的漏检语音，不该标却标的虚警语音，以及有人声但归错人的混淆，三者相加除以参考语音总时长。论文采用无宽容领、重叠计分的严格计分，对应国际上DIHARD确立的严格设置。读者需要先建立这个直觉：系统切得碎一点，漏检少但虚警多；切得整一点，虚警少但容易把停顿判成漏检，后文所有关于标注口径的讨论都围绕这个权衡展开。

[[CONCEPT_BRIDGE_1]]

sections.heading: 已有路线如何做日志，印度语料此前缺了哪一块
sections.body: 已有路线大致分两类。一类是模块式：先做语音检测，再对短片段提声纹向量，最后聚类，典型后端是基于贝叶斯隐马尔可夫模型的x向量聚类。另一类是端到端神经日志，直接逐帧预测多人活动，天然处理重叠；其中端到端加向量聚类的混合路线先在局部窗内做端到端分割，再用全局聚类把局部说话人串起来，从而支持任意时长和人数。幂集形式把局部多人活动看成对发声子集的单标签分类，是pyannote一系的基础；DiariZen把前端换成结构化剪枝的WavLM加Conformer，NVIDIA的Sortformer则按说话人出现顺序做监督。印度语言方面，此前大规模语料多面向识别和预训练，日志专用基准只有DISPLACE的几个语言，而IndicDiarBench第一次覆盖全部22种 scheduled 语言，共1164段约107.7小时，包含近场会议、远场会议和野外视频三类，参考由五阶段人工流程产生。论文的比较对象因此是专用日志系统，而不是同时做转写和日志的商用服务，后者在基准论文里已有自报数字，但作者并未重新运行它们。

sections.heading: 论文要解决的三个具体问题是什么
sections.body: 第一个问题是在同一协议下盲测最强专用日志系统在印度会话上的真实水平。盲测意味着所有系统都按各自推荐配置跑同一单声道音频，用同一计分器、同一无宽容领且重叠计分规则，不在基准上调参，本文系统同样冻结后才第一次在基准上计分。第二个问题是除声学之外还有什么决定误差。作者发现基准参考按转写话语切分，话语内短停顿不断开，而日志器按停顿切分，每个话语内停顿都会被计成漏检，这是一个与声音本身无关的口径差异。第三个问题是如何在22种语言上取得领先，同时不丢掉国际基准上的通用性。适应数据只有八种语言的双人电话，加上公开多方会议，检验的是印度信道和会话条件能否跨语系迁移，而不是为每种语言单独建模。这三个问题分别对应后文的系统对比、口径测量和印度适配，缺一不可。理解这三者的分工，才能明白为什么论文既要做大规模评测，又要做桥接分析和适配训练。

sections.heading: Anuvani-Diarization 的整体流程是什么
sections.body:
系统沿用端到端加向量聚类结构。音频统一为16kHz后，按16秒窗、1.6秒步长滑窗送入分割网络，网络每20毫秒输出一个幂集类别，共16类，对应窗内四个局部说话人的全部子集。取最大概率类别后做11帧中值滤波得到平滑的局部活动。对每个局部说话人，只用其无重叠帧提ResNet34声纹向量，要求至少有多于两帧无重叠帧才参与；再用VBx聚类把跨窗口的局部身份连成全局说话人，聚类沿用父模型的概率线性判别分析和默认参数。最后把帧级活动聚合成整段录音的谁在何时说话。网络之后没有任何调参，改动只发生在分割网络的印度适配上。推理是确定性的，重复运行按字节复现输出，分片与单卡重跑结果一致。

[[CONCEPT_BRIDGE_2]]

sections.heading: 分割网络内部如何从波形得到每帧类别
sections.body:
分割网络起点是DiariZen的WavLM-Large稀疏80%版本加四块Conformer头。WavLM-Large编码器原本有多层输出，网络学习25路输出的加权混合，再经1024到256线性层和层归一化进入Conformer。每个Conformer块内部按半步前馈、多头自注意力、卷积核长31的卷积模块、半步前馈、层归一化的顺序处理，前后层残差连接，四块结构相同。论文配图把其中一块展开，目的就是让研究生看到局部卷积抓停顿和音节边界，自注意力抓窗内说话人轮转，组合后输出每帧的16类分布。窗口内最多建模四个同时说话人，整段录音的人数不受限，因为人数由聚类阶段展开。嵌入模型是660万参数的ResNet34，分割网络本身6950万参数，聚类阶段用凝聚初始化阈值0.6和VBx迭代20次等父模型设置。

[[CONCEPT_BRIDGE_3]]

sections.heading: 嵌入和聚类如何把局部身份连成全局时间线
sections.body: 举一个例子帮助理解分工：一段16秒窗经网络得到每20毫秒的局部说话人0到3的活动，若0和1在某几百毫秒同时为1，即判为重叠。随后对0号说话人所有标为其单独发声的帧提声纹向量，重叠帧不用，避免混入他人音色。滑窗推进后，下一窗又出现局部身份，声纹向量在全局做VBx聚类，声纹接近的局部身份被归为同一全局人。不能连接的修复、阈值和迭代次数都沿用父模型，本文没有为基准重调。例子只是帮助理解分工：分割管何时有人和局部是谁，嵌入管声音像谁，聚类管跨窗对应，任何一环切得过碎或过整都会同时改变漏检、虚警和混淆的分配。这也解释了为什么只适配分割网络就能改变总体误差，而聚类保持冻结。

sections.heading: 印度适配用了哪些数据，不确定银标签如何构造
sections.body:
适配集共848段370.5小时。印度部分是SPRING-INX的302个双人电话，覆盖阿萨姆语、孟加拉语、古吉拉特语、印地语、马拉雅拉姆语、马拉地语、旁遮普语、泰米尔语八种语言，共98.5小时；多方会议部分是NOTSOFAR-1、AMI、AISHELL-4和AliMeeting。每批采样一半来自印度电话且语言均衡，四分之一来自NOTSOFAR-1，四分之一来自其他会议。关键是银标签的不确定性处理：电话每人一路信道，原则上可直接得标签，但串音、音量小、未转写语音都会让标签出错。作者把每10毫秒小格标为已知或未知，能量不支持、比另一路低15分贝以上、与转写区间矛盾、在标签或转写边界100毫秒内、与独立预训练日志器在隔离信道上的判断不一致，都标为未知，未知帧不贡献损失，安静的正标签被屏蔽而不是改成静音。98.5小时电话音频最后保留51.9小时有监督。训练用AdamW全参数联合微调3000步，每步96个16秒片段，共288000个片段，编码器学习率2e-6、头2e-5，50步热身后余弦衰减，梯度裁剪1.0，bf16运算，在六张RTX A6000上约91分钟。候选电话事先经声纹指纹加波形核验筛查，与基准无音频重叠。

[[CONCEPT_BRIDGE_4]]

sections.heading: 评测协议如何保证零样本和可复现
sections.body: 数据是IndicDiarBench的全部1164段录音，近场781段、远场173段、野外210段，说话人数2到8人的共1157段，另有7段9人仍计入总分。计分用NIST语义，与dscore在所查系统和集合上一致，并合并基准中少量同说话人重叠参考。报告两种聚合：池化错误率按参考语音时间加权，时长加权按录音时长加权，基准论文采用后者。置信区间来自对590个源录音的5000次自助重采样。对手是九个按各自推荐配置运行的系统，包括pyannoteAI Precision-2商用接口、DiariZen大模型版本、NVIDIA Nemotron-3等，多卡分片与单卡重跑按字节一致。零样本指本文分割网络只在非基准录音上适配，配方和检查点在内部非基准面板上固定，聚类用父模型默认设置，冻结后才第一次在基准上计分，对手均为开箱即用。需要区分的三件事是：代码、权重与可运行服务，本文权重在Hugging Face的链接本次未能确认可达，商用联合转写服务的数字是基准作者转述的自报值，并非作者重跑。

sections.heading: 分条件和分人数时优势在哪里消失
sections.body:
拆分比较的问题是：总体领先在不同录音条件和不同人数下是否稳定，比较对象是四个最强实际可运行系统，指标仍是越小越好。下表按近场、远场、野外和2到8人分组给出池化错误率，组大小差异很大，8人组只有26段，2人组有294段。

[[TABLE_2]]

分组结果显示领先存在明确边界。近场19.05%对19.93%、远场18.64%对19.48%本文领先，野外11.51%落后于pyannoteAI的10.78%，这是总体结论的第一个反例。人数上除4人组外2到8人均领先，但人数分组同时混入了录音内容和时长的差异，只能描述观测分组的表现，不能理解为向同一会话加人后的因果效应。换句话说，方法更适合多人辩论式近远场会议，在野外视频上不占优，不能把总体领先推广到所有场景。

sections.heading: 人数曲线和条件柱状图如何补充表格
sections.body:
下图把上一节的拆分画成曲线和柱子，左图横轴是参考人数，纵轴是池化错误率，右图按三类条件分组，柱子从左到右依次是父模型、Nemotron、pyannoteAI和本文系统。读图时先沿2到8人看四条折线的上扬趋势，再按三组比较蓝色柱子的高低。

[[FIGURE_5]]

图后解释可见：左图四条线都随人数增加上扬，本文曲线在大部分人数上最低，但在4人处被反超；右图近场和远场蓝色柱最低，野外蓝色柱高于pyannoteAI。曲线的上扬本身不证明人数是唯一原因，因为不同人数的录音内容和重叠率也不同。结合表格，结论是印度适配在近远场多方会议上稳定获益，但在野外视频上存在明确短板，这为后文讨论训练数据只有电话和会议、缺少野外视频埋下伏笔。

sections.heading: 标注口径为什么是隐藏变量，桥接实验说明了什么
sections.body:
口径问题的起点是同说话人间隙分布。基准参考中小于0.5秒的同说话人间隙只占7.7%，近场仅3.4%，而四个日志器输出中占24.9%到32.1%，说明系统按停顿切，参考按话语切，每个话语内停顿都会被计成漏检。桥接分析保持声学判决不变，只把小于阈值的同说话人间隙填上，阈值在基准上事后选取，属于口径测量而非可用系统。读图说明：左图是间隙占比条形，右图横轴是桥接阈值、纵轴是池化错误率，实线是四个系统桥接后的变化，虚线是电话口径适配后的本文系统。

[[FIGURE_3]]

图后解释需要区分测量与系统：桥接让四个系统分别下降1.90、2.03、2.91和4.14个百分点，切得最碎的Nemotron获益最大；同一桥接用在词对齐的VoxConverse、NOTSOFAR-1和MagicData-RAMC上反而上升0.68到6.01个百分点。因此没有口径无关的输出，话语级适合按人归属文字，词对齐适合声学分析，基准应像记录领和重叠规则一样记录切分口径，系统比较只能在匹配口径下进行。虚线整体抬高则预告了下一节电话口径迁移失败的结果。

[[CONCEPT_BRIDGE_5]]

sections.heading: 印度适配带来多少增益，电话口径为什么学不来
sections.body:
本表比较的问题是：印度适配相对父模型改变了什么，以及在电话转写上学到的桥接口径能否搬到基准上，所有行都是零样本计分，最后一行按预先固定协议只在基准上评一次。下表三行分别是父模型、加印度适配、再加电话口径，列出池化、时长加权和三类误差。

[[TABLE_3]]

表后解释要同时讲收益和失败。印度适配把池化从18.31%降到17.11%，时长加权从17.99%降到16.78%，漏检从11.07%降到8.91%，代价是虚警增加0.52个百分点、混淆增加0.43个百分点，属于用少量虚警换大量漏检。电话口径行把漏检压到2.89%，但虚警涨到15.29%，总误差涨到池化22.74%、时长加权22.43%。原因是电话转写员把话语开得更长，桥接在1.5秒仍有效，而基准话语在0.8到1.0秒就饱和，两个同样是话语级转写的话语终点定义仍不一致。这是一个有证据的负结果：不经过同方式产生的参考，就学不会该基准的口径，事后阈值也不能当成部署可得的提升。

sections.heading: 国际基准上的通用性有没有丢失
sections.body:
通用性比较的问题是：为印度适配的分割网络在六个国际测试集上是否退化，两个系统共用父模型聚类，只换分割网络，因此比较的是分割网络本身的效果。下表给出每个测试集的文件数和双方错误率，平均是对测试集等权，不是按录音或时长池化。

[[TABLE_4]]

平均结果没有显示通用性受损。平均12.03%对父模型12.19%，三升三降，最大改善在NOTSOFAR-1上0.85个百分点，最大回退在MagicData-RAMC上0.16个百分点，平均没有损害通用性。但平均等权掩盖了每集方向不同，不能说每组都不退化；而且国际结果只是第二视角，不是印度视角，不能替代在印度多方会议和野外视频上的验证。结合前文，适配学到的更可能是印度信道和会话条件，而非特定语言属性，这仍是推测，需要控制实验验证。

sections.heading: 哪些结论还不成立，哪些范围尚未评测
sections.body: 第一，本文没有建模基准的话语口径，匹配它可再降约1.9个百分点，但作者没有在基准上拟合它，电话学习路径已证伪。第二，时长加权仍高于Sarvam自报0.78个百分点，且对方系统未被重跑，不能断言专用系统已全面超越联合服务。第三，分割窗内最多四个同时说话人，全局人数虽不限，极端重叠和九人录音的证据很少，全文1157段2到8人之外只有7段9人。第四，印度适配只有八种语言的双人电话，多方印度会议训练可能进一步有帮助，十种未见语言上的领先提示学到的是印度信道和会话条件，但这仍是推测。第五，评估只有一个108小时基准，国际结果只是第二视角。部署前必须在自己的语言、信道和人数分布上重测，不能把平均趋势套到每一组。

sections.heading: 复现第一步做什么，需要哪些版本和许可
sections.body: 第一步是按原文版本固定环境和数据修订：IndicDiarBench的Hugging Face修订、PyTorch 2.1.1、pyannote.audio 3.1.1的DiariZen代码库提交、scikit-learn和NumPy版本，以及父模型权重和声纹模型的许可。注意许可分开：基准CC BY 4.0，父分割权重CC BY-NC 4.0只允许非商业研究，对手系统各按自有条款，商用接口与可下载权重是两回事。推理按16秒窗、1.6秒步长、最大概率加11帧中值滤波、无重叠帧提向量、凝聚初始化后VBx的流程跑，关闭TF32、固定种子、每文件重置以保证确定性。补充材料称包含分数文件和重画图表脚本，可先从分数文件复算池化和时长加权，再重跑推理核对按字节一致。口径实验只需在输出后桥接同说话人间隙，不要重训网络。容易误解的是把事后桥接的下降当成系统提升，它只是测量口径的灵敏度分析。

sections.heading: 什么时候值得尝试，还缺哪项验证
sections.body: 当任务是印度多语言会议或电话的按人归属文字，且评价采用话语级参考时，值得尝试这种印度适配的分割加VBx路线，因为它在近远场和多数语言上收回漏检，且国际平均没有退化。当任务是声学边界分析或词对齐基准时，不应直接套用话语级桥接，否则虚警会大涨。还缺的验证是同方式产生的基准口径标注：要么在基准风格的参考上学习显式口径模式，要么把口径做成可切换的文档化选项，而不是静默采用一种切分。另一个缺口是多方印度会议训练和野外视频的针对性改进，因为当前领先不包括野外组。复现时先固定版本和许可，再从分数文件复算指标，最后才重跑推理；任何新场景都要重测自己的语言、信道和人数分布。

cases.sourceText:
Anuvani-Diarization: Zero Shot Speaker Diarization
and Annotation Conventions Across 22 Languages
Stephen Fernandes
Affiliation: Central Institute of Indian Languages
Narayan Choudhary
Affiliation: stephenn.fernandes@gmail.com, n.choudhary@gov.in
Abstract
India’s 22 scheduled languages are spoken by over a billion people in conversations that mix languages, often within one turn, overlap freely, and take place over telephones, in meetings, and in media. Knowing who spoke when, the task of speaker diarization, is essential to speech applications for such conversation: voice agents conversing with several people at once, speaker attributed transcription of meetings and calls, contact center analytics, and media monitoring. We present a systematic study of speaker diarization across all 22 languages on IndicDiarBench and introduce Anuvani-Diarization, which adapts a self-supervised end-to-end segmentation model to Indian conversation with uncertainty aware silver supervision. Evaluated zero shot alongside nine recent diarization systems, it reaches a duration weighted diarization error rate (DER) of 16.78% on all 1,164 recordings, the lowest of all systems we ran and second only to the best published result (16.0%), and leads the three strongest rivals in 14 of 22 languages. It matches its parent on six international benchmarks. We also show that the benchmark’s utterance level annotation convention is a hidden variable worth 1.9 to 4.1 DER points, depending on the system, and that a convention learned from other Indian transcriptions does not transfer.
Figure 1: Anuvani-Diarization on Indic DiarBench and global benchmarks. DER (%); bars start at zero.
The released model is available at:
 https://huggingface.co/CIIL/Anuvani-Diarization
1 Introduction
Conversation in India is multilingual by default. The Constitution recognizes 22 languages in its Eighth Schedule (Ministry of Home Affairs, 2017), the 2011 Census recorded 19,569 raw mother tongue returns and found that 96.71% of the population has a scheduled language as its mother tongue (Registrar General of India, 2018), and roughly a quarter of the population reports speaking a second language (Sarma, 2025). Speakers move between languages within a single turn (Gumperz, 1982; Bali et al., 2014), interject, and overlap, and the same conversation may be held over a telephone, a video call or around a table. Every downstream technology that attributes words to people, from meeting transcription to broadcast monitoring and call analytics, first needs to answer the fundamental question of who spoke when.
Until recently there was no benchmark that could measure this capability across India’s languages. The DISPLACE challenges introduced diarization of code mixed Indian conversation only for a handful of languages (Baghel et al., 2023; Kalluri et al., 2024), and IndicDiarBench (Mehendale et al., 2026) now provides 108 hours of human corrected, speaker attributed conversation in all 22 scheduled languages, recorded as near field meetings, far field meetings and in-the-wild video. Its first results came from services that transcribe and diarize jointly, the strongest at a diarization error rate (DER) of 16.0%; dedicated diarization systems, which most research and deployment build on, were not evaluated.
We ask how the strongest diarization systems perform on Indian conversation when measured blind under one protocol, what, beyond acoustics, determines their errors, and what it would take to lead across the 22 languages. Our contributions are:
• 
A blind evaluation of nine diarization systems on all 1,164 IndicDiarBench recordings, with two independent scorer implementations, bootstrap intervals over source recordings and byte identical sharded inference (§4).
• 
Annotation convention as a hidden variable. The references segment speech the way transcribers do, into utterances; diarizers segment it at pauses. The gap moves every system by 1.9–4.1 pp of DER and the same correction is harmful on word aligned benchmarks, so convention must be an explicit property of a diarizer’s output; a convention learned from Indian telephone transcriptions does not transfer to the benchmark (§5).
• 
Anuvani-Diarization, an Indic adaptation of a self-supervised end-to-end segmentation model with uncertainty aware silver supervision from channel separated telephone calls (§6). Evaluated zero shot, with no part fitted or selected on the benchmark, it reaches 16.78% duration weighted DER, the lowest of all systems we ran (Figure 2), and leads the three strongest other systems in 14 of the 22 languages (Table 1).
• 
Generality: the adapted network matches its parent on six international benchmarks (§7.4).
Figure 2: Anuvani-Diarization is the most accurate of all systems we ran on IndicDiarBench. Duration weighted DER on all 1,164 recordings (zero collar, overlap scored). †Joint transcription and diarization services reported by the benchmark’s authors (Mehendale et al., 2026); all others were run under our protocol (Table 3).
2 Diarizing India: A Linguistic Perspective
Diarization is usually treated as a language independent task: a speaker’s voice is assumed to be the same regardless of the language they speak. India tests this assumption in four ways.
Scale and diversity.
The 22 scheduled languages range from Hindi, the mother tongue of 528.3 million people (43.63% of the population), to Sanskrit, returned as a mother tongue by 24,821 people (Registrar General of India, 2018). Eleven of them have more than thirty million mother tongue speakers each. The country’s Greenberg diversity index is 0.930: two randomly chosen residents would almost always have different native languages (Sarma, 2025). IndicDiarBench mirrors this distribution only partly. Eight of its languages (Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Marathi, Punjabi, Tamil and Telugu) each contribute about four hours of near field meetings and appear in far field and in-the-wild recordings, while the fourteen others contribute about 1.5 hours of near field meetings each, and twelve of them appear in no other condition (Mehendale et al., 2026). A diarizer for India must therefore work well on languages for which almost no conversational training data exists.
Four families, one linguistic area.
The scheduled languages belong to four families: fifteen are Indo-Aryan, four Dravidian (Kannada, Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu), two Tibeto-Burman (Bodo, Manipuri) and one Austroasiatic (Santali); they are written in more than ten scripts (Table 1). Centuries of contact have made South Asia a linguistic area in which unrelated languages share structural and phonetic features (Emeneau, 1956; Masica, 1976), most audibly the contrast between retroflex and dental consonants and, in Indo-Aryan, a four way laryngeal contrast among stops (Ladefoged and Maddieson, 1996). Some features are local: Punjabi has lexical tone (Hussain et al., 2020), and Manipuri (Meitei) contrasts high and low lexical tones (Chelliah, 1997). Pitch and timing, two cues that speaker embedding models exploit, thus carry linguistic as well as personal information. Even the English spoken in these conversations is shaped by the speaker’s first language (Kachru, 1983; Sirsa and Redford, 2013). For speaker diarization, this means that a speaker model trained mostly on English must separate who is speaking from which language, and which variety of English, is being spoken.
Conversational practice.
Multilingual speakers switch languages within a given conversation for discourse purposes (Gumperz, 1982), and Hindi English mixing reaches into almost every register (Bali et al., 2014; Sitaram et al., 2019). IndicDiarBench’s annotators transcribe this mixing explicitly, and its authors describe the corpus as rich in “English code mixing, dialectal variation, and frequent speaker overlap” (Mehendale et al., 2026). Turn taking is universal in its basic organization but culturally variable when it comes to timing (Sacks et al., 1974; Stivers et al., 2009; Levinson, 2016): transitions that occur between speakers are short, and a substantial share of them have overlaps rather than gaps (Heldner and Edlund, 2010). In IndicDiarBench this share of overlapped speech varies from 6.1% (Punjabi) to 24.7% (Maithili) across languages; in-the-wild video has the least overlap (6.5%), and near field meetings, whose participants were given debate topics, have the most overlap (Mehendale et al., 2026).
The utterance as a unit of annotation.
Most importantly for this paper, a diarization reference embodies a theory of what a turn is. Word aligned references, typically derived from forced alignment, place segment boundaries at acoustic pauses. IndicDiarBench’s references are built by professional transcribers who correct speaker attributed, segment level transcriptions (Mehendale et al., 2026); their unit is the transcribed utterance, and short pauses which are within an utterance are not considered segment boundaries. Section 5 shows that this linguistic choice, rather than any acoustic property, is one of the largest single factors in diarization error on the benchmark.

3 Related Work
Diarization models.
Modular diarization systems detect speech, embed short segments and cluster the embeddings, with Bayesian HMM clustering of x-vectors (VBx) as a strong back end (Landini et al., 2022; Park et al., 2022). End-to-end neural diarization (EEND) predicts speaker activities jointly and processes overlap natively (Fujita et al., 2019); EEND with vector clustering (EEND-VC) combines local end-to-end segmentation with global clustering, so that recordings of any length and speaker count can be processed effectively (Kinoshita et al., 2021). The powerset formulation casts local segmentation as single label classification over subsets of active speakers (Plaquet and Bredin, 2023) and underlies pyannote (Bredin, 2023; pyannote, 2025); DiariZen replaces its front end with a structurally pruned WavLM (Chen et al., 2022; Han et al., 2025a; Han et al., 2025b) and a Conformer (Gulati et al., 2020). NVIDIA Sortformer models are trained explicitly with arrival-time-ordered speaker supervision (Park et al., 2024; Medennikov et al., 2025), the approach of NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Diarization (NVIDIA, 2026).
Evaluation conventions.
DER is sensitive to how references are made. Benchmarks differ in forgiveness collars and in whether overlap is scored; DIHARD established the strict setting of no collar with overlap scored (Ryant et al., 2021), and the underlying scoring tools differ in how they treat overlapping same speaker references (Bredin, 2017; Ryant, 2018). Most closely related to our analysis, Horiguchi et al. (2026b) decompose DER into a pause attributable component and a core component, and recent work trains models toward tight segment boundaries (Horiguchi et al., 2026a). We complement this line by measuring the convention of a multilingual benchmark directly, by showing that its effect is large and system wide, and by testing whether a convention learned from other transcriptions transfers to it.
Speech technology for Indian languages.
Large data collection efforts have produced corpora and benchmarks for Indian languages, including IndicVoices (Javed et al., 2024), Kathbath and IndicSUPERB (Javed et al., 2023), IndicWav2Vec (Javed et al., 2021), SPRING-INX (Nithya R et al., 2023) and the MahaDhwani pre-training corpus (Bhogale et al., 2025); code switched recognition has its own challenge series (Diwan et al., 2021). For diarization, DISPLACE 2023 provided 32 hours of code mixed conversation and DISPLACE 2024 158 hours, 38 of them labeled, in five Indian languages (Baghel et al., 2023; Kalluri et al., 2024; Mehendale et al., 2026); IndicDiarBench is the first benchmark to cover all 22 scheduled languages (Mehendale et al., 2026).
Concurrent work.
A related concurrent study evaluates spoken language identification across Indian languages, with emphasis on short-input robustness, calibration and language confusion (Fernandes and Choudhary, 2026). Its prediction target is the language of an audio segment. In contrast, this work predicts speaker activity over time and studies diarization error and annotation conventions. The two studies share their authors and build on publicly released Indian speech corpora; the public SPRING-INX corpus appears in both (as adaptation data here, as a held-out evaluation set there). Their pretrained backbones, benchmarks and experiments are otherwise distinct. The contributions and evaluations concern different speech-processing tasks.
4 Benchmark and Evaluation Protocol
Data.
IndicDiarBench contains 1,164 recordings (107.7 hours) with 2 to 9 speakers each: near field meetings recorded over an online platform with one close microphone per participant (about 53 hours, all 22 languages), far field meetings (27 hours, eight languages) and in-the-wild YouTube conversations (28 hours, ten languages). These meetings involve 485 speakers from 189 districts; references come from a five stage human pipeline (Mehendale et al., 2026). We use the Hugging Face release at revision 92877ba.
Scoring.
We follow the benchmark: DER with no collar and overlapped speech scored. We score with NIST md-eval semantics (our scorer is identical to dscore (Ryant, 2018) on every system and set we checked); the scorer merges the small number of overlapping same speaker reference segments in the benchmark. We report both pooled (micro) DER and the duration weighted average used by the benchmark paper. Competitor systems.
We ran nine diarization systems on the same single channel audio with each project’s recommended configuration: pyannoteAI Precision-2 through its commercial API (pyannoteAI, 2026), DiariZen WavLM-Large s80 md-v2 (Han et al., 2025a), NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Diarization (NVIDIA, 2026), pyannote speaker-diarization-community-1 (pyannote, 2025), NVIDIA Streaming Sortformer 4-speaker v2.1 and NVIDIA Sortformer 4-speaker v1 (Park et al., 2024; Medennikov et al., 2025), DiCoW v3.3 (BUT Speech@FIT, 2025), the 3D-Speaker pipeline (Chen et al., 2024) and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize (MOSI.AI et al., 2026). All outputs were scored together. For the systems that we ran on several GPUs, a single GPU replay of all 1,164 recordings reproduced the sharded outputs byte for byte.
Zero shot protocol.
Nothing in our system, Anuvani-Diarization, was trained, tuned or selected on IndicDiarBench. The segmentation network was adapted on other recordings (§6), audio fingerprint screening found no audio shared with the benchmark, the recipe and checkpoint were fixed on an internal panel of non-benchmark recordings, and its clustering uses the parent model’s default settings. The system was frozen before it was first scored on the benchmark, although earlier versions of it had been scored there. The competitor systems were run off the shelf, so every system we report was evaluated zero shot.
5 Annotation Convention as a Hidden Variable

Diagnosis.
Figure 3 (left) compares gaps between consecutive same speaker segments. In IndicDiarBench’s references only 7.7% of such gaps are shorter than half a second, and only 3.4% in the near field meetings. In the output of every diarizer in Figure 3 (left), the share is between 24.9% and 32.1%. The systems are not wrong about the acoustics: speakers tend to pause inside their turns. They disagree with the references about what counts as a segment, and every such pause inside a reference utterance is scored as missed speech.

Bridging same speaker gaps shorter than a threshold gg is a convention change that leaves the acoustic decisions untouched. Its effect is large and consistent (Figure 3, right; Table 2). A property of the benchmark, not of speech.
Applied to benchmarks whose references are word aligned, the same bridging raises DER, by 0.68 to 6.01 pp on VoxConverse, NOTSOFAR-1 and MagicData-RAMC (Table 2, bottom). There is therefore no convention free output: the best segmentation depends on whose notion of a turn is being scored. Utterance level references suit speaker attributed transcription and word aligned references acoustic analysis, and neither is wrong. We draw three consequences: benchmarks should document their segmentation conventions as precisely as their collar and overlap rules; systems should be compared only under matched output conventions; and a diarizer should expose its convention as an explicit, documented mode rather than silently adopting one.
5.1 Learning an annotation convention
Can the convention be learned without the benchmark’s labels? We fitted a convention decoder on human transcriptions of 302 SPRING-INX telephone calls, which, like the benchmark’s references, are speaker attributed utterance spans; chose every setting on 35 held out calls under a protocol fixed in advance; and scored the frozen system once on all 1,164 recordings. DER rose from 17.11% to 22.74% (Table 4): missed speech fell from 8.91% to 2.89%, but false alarm rose from 3.55% to 15.29%. On the telephone transcripts, bridging kept helping up to the largest gap we allowed (1.5 s): their transcribers keep an utterance open across longer pauses than the benchmark’s annotators do. Two corpora that both segment speech into transcribed utterances thus still disagree about where an utterance ends, so a diarizer can match a benchmark’s convention only from references produced the same way.
Selection protocol.
A protocol fixing every candidate and decision rule was committed before any measurement, and a filesystem guard refused every IndicDiarBench file to the selection code. For this experiment only, clustering was chosen on 146 recordings of NOTSOFAR-1, VoxConverse, SPRING-INX, AMI, AISHELL-4 and AliMeeting from 21 VBx configurations, with and without a cannot-link repair that splits clusters whose strongly supported local speakers share a window; the repair at threshold 0.65 and Fa=0.06F_{a}=0.06 won (mean pooled DER 12.26% against 12.51% for the default).
Decoder training.
References for the convention were the human transcript spans of each SPRING-INX call’s two channels. The bridging gap was chosen on 35 held out calls from g∈{0,0.25,…,1.5}g\in\{0,0.25,\dots,1.5\} s (best: 1.5 s). The decoder, gradient boosted regression trees (Ke et al., 2017; Pedregosa et al., 2011) with 400 iterations, learning rate 0.05, 31 leaves and at least 200 samples per leaf, predicts for every same speaker gap and every segment shorter than 3 s the change in error time that bridging the gap or dropping the segment would cause, from the local geometry, the recording and the network’s own evidence.
Held-out selection and final evaluation.
Fitted on the 302 training calls, it beat blanket bridging on the 35 held out calls (duration weighted DER 30.02% against 32.11%, paired 95% CI entirely below zero) and was adopted. The frozen system was scored once on IndicDiarBench: 22.74% pooled and 22.43% duration weighted DER.

The inset opens one Conformer block. Overlap-free speaker embeddings and VBx clustering link local speakers across windows; chips summarise the adaptation recipe.
Anuvani-Diarization follows the EEND-VC design (Figure 4). A segmentation network processes 16 s windows with a 1.6 s hop and predicts, for every 20 ms frame, one of 16 powerset classes over four local speakers. Overlap free frames of each local speaker are embedded with a ResNet34 speaker model (He et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2023), local speakers are linked across windows by VBx clustering with the parent model’s probabilistic linear discriminant analysis (PLDA) and default settings, and the frame level activities are aggregated into a recording level segmentation. Nothing after the network is tuned.
Starting point.
We start from DiariZen WavLM-Large s80 md-v2, whose segmentation network combines a WavLM-Large encoder pruned to 80% sparsity with a Conformer head (Han et al., 2025a; Han et al., 2025b), and adapt it to Indian conversational speech.
Data.
The adaptation set contains 848 recordings (370.5 hours). Indian conversation comes from 302 two party telephone calls of SPRING-INX in eight languages (Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Tamil; 98.5 hours) (Nithya R et al., 2023). Multi-party meetings come from NOTSOFAR-1 (71 recordings, 7.3 hours) (Vinnikov et al., 2024), AMI (101, 59.9 hours) (Carletta et al., 2005), AISHELL-4 (173, 97.2 hours) (Fu et al., 2021) and AliMeeting (201, 107.6 hours) (Yu et al., 2022). Each mini-batch draws 50% of its crops from the Indian calls with languages balanced, 25% from NOTSOFAR-1 and 25% from the other meetings. The 302 calls are 90 calls admitted first and 212 of 346 later candidates: before admission, every candidate was screened against every other recording by acoustic fingerprinting (Lalinský, 2010) with waveform corroboration, the 134 candidates that matched another recording were held out, and no audio in the adaptation set is shared with the benchmark.
Silver labels with explicit uncertainty.
Each SPRING-INX call was recorded with one channel per speaker, which yields speaker labels without manual annotation, but channel evidence is imperfect: a quiet speaker, crosstalk or untranscribed speech can make a label wrong. Rather than trusting or discarding such labels, we mark every 10 ms cell as known or unknown. A cell is unknown if a positive label lacks energy support on its own channel, is more than 15 dB quieter than the other channel, contradicts a transcript interval, falls within 100 ms of a label or transcript boundary, or disagrees with an independent pretrained diarizer applied to each isolated channel. Unknown frames contribute no loss; quiet positives are masked rather than relabeled as silence. Of the 98.5 hours of call audio, 51.9 hours remain supervised.
Training.
We train all parameters jointly for 3,000 updates of 96 sixteen second crops each (288,000 crops) with AdamW (β=(0.9,0.98)\beta=(0.9,0.98), weight decay 0.01), learning rates of 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} for the encoder and 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} for the head, 50 warmup updates, cosine decay, gradient clipping at 1.0 and bfloat16 arithmetic. Training takes about 91 minutes on six RTX A6000 GPUs.
Size.
The network has 69.5 M parameters and the speaker model 6.6 M. Inference is deterministic: rerunning it reproduces its outputs byte for byte.

7 Results
7.1 Overall benchmark performance
Table 3 and Figure 2 show that Anuvani-Diarization reaches 17.11% pooled and 16.78% duration weighted DER on all 1,164 recordings (pooled 95% CI: 15.80 to 18.45), the lowest of all systems we ran. The paired bootstrap differences all exclude zero: −-0.47 pp (95% CI [−-0.84, −-0.09]) against pyannoteAI Precision-2, −-1.21 ([−-1.40, −-1.01]) against DiariZen md-v2 and −-1.60 ([−-2.18, −-1.06]) against NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Diarization. The only lower published figure is the 16.0% self-reported by Sarvam AI for its joint transcription and diarization service, 0.78 pp below ours in duration weighted terms. Every system is a single trained model, so the intervals reflect the sampling of recordings, not training seeds.

8 Discussion
Convention is part of the task.
The convention adapter failed for a reason that supports Section 5: two corpora transcribed into speaker attributed utterances still disagree about where an utterance ends. Matching a benchmark’s convention therefore needs references made the way the benchmark’s are, or a convention documented precisely enough to be reproduced.
Linguistic diversity and transfer.
Anuvani-Diarization’s Indian adaptation data covers eight languages of two party telephone conversation, yet ten of the fourteen languages in which it leads are languages it never saw in adaptation, including Manipuri, Sanskrit, Urdu and Santali. This suggests that the adaptation mostly teaches the acoustic and conversational conditions of Indian speech, which transfer across the families of the linguistic area, rather than properties of particular languages. Difficulty remains where conversation is hardest: near field debates with many participants and over 20% overlapped speech, as in Nepali, Telugu, Maithili and Dogri.
9 Conclusion
We presented the first systematic study of dedicated speaker diarization systems across India’s 22 scheduled languages, showed that the benchmark’s utterance level convention is a hidden variable worth 1.9 to 4.1 pp of DER and that a convention learned from other transcriptions does not transfer to it, and introduced Anuvani-Diarization, which, evaluated zero shot, is the most accurate of all systems we ran (16.78% duration weighted DER) and matches its parent across six international benchmarks.
Limitations
Anuvani-Diarization does not model the benchmark’s segmentation convention: matching it would lower its DER by about 1.9 pp (Table 2), but our attempt to learn it from other transcriptions failed (§5.1), and we did not fit it on the benchmark itself. Its duration weighted DER remains 0.78 pp above the 16.0% self-reported by Sarvam AI, whose system we did not run. The segmentation network models at most four simultaneous speakers within a 16 s window, although the number of speakers per recording is unbounded. The Indian adaptation data comprises two party telephone calls in eight languages; multi-party Indian meetings for training would likely help further. Our evaluation uses one benchmark of 108 hours; the international results provide a second view but not an Indian one. The network inherits the non-commercial license (CC BY-NC 4.0) of its parent model’s weights.
Ethical Considerations
All training and evaluation data are publicly released research corpora, used under their terms of release; no new recordings of people were made. Diarization identifies when different people speak but not who they are; it can nevertheless be combined with other tools to profile speakers, and the model’s weights are licensed for non-commercial research use only. Performance varies across languages and conditions (Table 1); deployments should evaluate on their own population.

conceptBridges.explanation: 口语语种识别指只听音频判断整段话属于23类中哪一类，为后续选识别器和翻译方向提供路由依据；macro-F1指先在每个语言上算F1再平均，它让小语种和大语种权重相同，所以论文用它做主指标，避免大语种掩盖尾部语言的错误。
Conformer编码器指把卷积和自注意力交替堆叠的语音特征提取器，负责把80维对数Mel特征变成逐帧的上下文表示；注意力统计池化指对所有帧学权重再取加权均值和标准差拼成定长向量，负责把变长语音压成一句的语种向量，二者搭配实现从变长波形到定长分类输入的转换。
焦点损失指按样本难易给损失加权，让已分对的简单样本梯度衰减、难样本主导更新，解决样本难度不均；温度采样指按语言数据量的1/T次方决定抽到各语言的概率，解决语言频次不均；前者管一次看到后怎么算，后者管多 often看到谁，组合后兼顾头部曝光和尾部召回。
混淆簇课程指训练前期压低15个印欧雅利安语的采样权重、后期恢复到正常配比，让模型先学大区分再学近亲区分；权重平均汤指把训练轨迹上不同时刻的7个检查点在参数空间直接平均，保留早期检查点的信道鲁棒性和后期检查点的短语音鲁棒性，推理时仍是一个模型，不增加计算量。
期望校准误差指把预测置信度分箱后比较平均置信度和实际准确率的差距，衡量置信度是否可信；最大softmax拒绝指用输出概率的最大值作为是否属于已知23类的分数，低分则拒识；前者管已知类内部分数能否用于路由和拒识阈值，后者管未知音乐、非印度语言能否被挡住。

sections.heading: 多语语音管线为什么先要判断语种
sections.body:
口语语种识别的输入是一段16kHz语音波形，目标是输出这段话属于哪一种语言，论文固定为23类：印度宪法第八附表所列22种语言加印度口音英语。识别结果决定后面调用哪个语音识别器、翻译方向选什么、客服电话用什么语言应答，一旦送错，例如把迈蒂利语送进印地语识别器，后面所有模块都会连带变差。印度场景的难点在于语种多且亲缘近，部署音频往往很短、带噪声、经电话窄带传输，还常有语码混合。日常语言中的语种识别指听声辨种，macro-F1指每个语言单独算F1再取平均，数值越高越好，大小语种权重相等。

[[CONCEPT_BRIDGE_1]]

论文先验证了一个流行假设是否成立：基础语音模型是否已经把语种识别当作内在的泛化能力解决了。作者用完全相同的音频片段测试发现，Whisper只有23类中15类的语言标识，1秒输入下Gemini 3.5 Flash只有0.52的macro-F1，GPT-audio只有0.14。这说明在印度语言上，通用大模型的覆盖不全、短语音崩塌、分数不可直接用于路由，因此仍需要一个小而专用且分数可信的模型。

sections.heading: 已有语种识别路线与本文的对照位置
sections.body:
传统路线从i向量到x向量再到ECAPA-TDNN，常用VoxLingua107这类百余语种数据训练开放基线。近年自监督语音编码器占优，包括XLS-R、MMS系列，以及在wav2vec 2.0风格模型上微调的专用模型，还有微调自监督Conformer的做法。NIST语言识别评测强调用簇感知的Cavg等指标。印度语言方面，IIITH-ILSC最早给出23类基准，后续有用CTC特征或微调XLSR-53的工作，但核心困难是跨语料泛化，有研究报道等错误率从语料内11.8%升到跨语料43.3%，声学增强只能挽回一部分。

本文与上述工作的输入输出相同，都是波形进、语种标签出，但监督规模和评测方式不同：训练池做到54,643小时、31.24M条、18个语料，覆盖全部23个口语类；评测先重建了102个条件的基准，强调说话人和语料双重 held-out，而不是只报干净域内准确率。与MMS自带4017语言头、Whisper解码器先吐语言标识、音频大语言模型提示后说出语言名相比，本文是把预训练Conformer全量微调为专用分类器，再与15个开放和商用系统在相同片段上对比。

sections.heading: 印度23类的语言学难点具体难在哪
sections.body:
按论文整理的23类，语系上15个印欧雅利安语、4个达罗毗荼语、2个藏缅语、1个南亚语系，另加印度英语。人口与训练量严重错位：训练音频从印度口音英语的13,039小时到克什米尔语的369小时，乌尔都语母语超5,000万人但音频少于迈蒂利语和尼泊尔语。标签本身是行政划分，人口普查的印地语合并了56种母语，迈蒂利语2001年前还计在印地语下，所以类边界部分是人为约定。

声音上的可分线索很稀疏。文字在语音中不存在，天城体至少服务10个类别，印地语和乌尔都语口语相近但文字不同，靠转写无法区分。剩下的靠卷舌程度、送气与浊音对立、元音长短、旁遮普语等4种语言的声调、信德语内爆音等罕见音段。亲缘对直接造成混淆：印地语与乌尔都语共享口语体，旁遮普语与多格里语基本词汇共享93%，孔卡尼语与马拉地语曾被视为方言，阿萨姆语、孟加拉语、奥里亚语同属一支。印度英语本身吸收了19种母语口音，每句英语都带着需要同时识别的那些语言的痕迹。1秒片段可能一个关键线索都不包含，这解释了为什么时长是比噪声更主导的难度轴。

sections.heading: Anuvani-LID从波形到23类的整体流程
sections.body:
模型输入是16kHz音频，先算80维对数Mel特征，窗长25毫秒、帧移10毫秒，再经4倍卷积下采样到40毫秒一帧。接着进入已在279k小时印度音频上自监督预训练的MahaDhwani Conformer-L编码器，共17个Conformer块，每块维度512、8头、卷积核31。17个块的输出用一组可学习的权重加权混合，再做注意力统计池化得到1024维的均值加标准差表示，压缩到256维嵌入，最后经23路分类器输出。训练用焦点损失加0.1标签平滑，总参数115.6M，整个网络全量微调。

推理时对每段音频只前向一次，直接在23类上取最大概率。论文还用开发集拟合了一个温度系数0.674做温度缩放，只改变置信度大小，不改变排序和预测类别。最终发布的是训练轨迹上7个检查点的参数平均，不是多模型集成，因此推理代价与单个模型相同。

sections.heading: 编码器、层混合与池化各自负责什么
sections.body:
编码器负责把声学帧变成带上下文的表示，预训练已见过大量印度语音，但顶层更服务预训练目标，线性探测显示语言信息在预训练时集中在第9到11块，到17块反而塌到0.13左右。全量微调后峰值移到第11到12块，54.6k小时模型在第12块达0.86，说明语言判别需要中上层而非最底层。层混合指对17个块输出学一组softmax权重再加权求和，让模型同时用多层信息，论文发现全量模型给第17块约30%权重，其余主要在10到16块，单块敲除代价不超过0.08，鲁棒性来自多层互补。

[[CONCEPT_BRIDGE_2]]

池化和损失的选择来自第一阶段25个对照：在1,000小时、20语言、4轮的相同 recipe 下，统计池化、多头、NetVLAD、ECAPA-TDNN等池化在跨语料macro-F1上都在0.825到0.837之间，差距约1个百分点且区间重叠；但损失决定校准，余弦间隔头的期望校准误差高达0.75到0.79，而softmax头只有0.02到0.08。注意力池化加焦点损失以0.840居首且校准好，ECAPA深头多2,300万参数仍未超过它，因此保留最简单的单网络结构。

sections.heading: 采样、增强、课程与优化如何分工训练
sections.body:
采样解决语言不均。论文用语言数据量的1/T次方决定抽样比，T越大越偏向均匀。在4,000小时保持生产分布的代理集上，跨语料macro-F1随T呈倒U形，T=2时0.919，T=1时0.890，均匀时0.898；T从1升到2，500小时以下语言平均F1从0.742升到0.930，而2,000小时以上语言仅从0.949滑到0.935。最终全量用T=1.75，并给英语16%、印地语11%的下限，防止头部在焦点损失下曝光不足。

[[CONCEPT_BRIDGE_3]]

增强解决条件覆盖。波形按固定顺序依次做变速、正负15dB的MUSAN噪声、6万条房间脉冲混响、时长裁剪、1到6人babble、8kHz G.711窄带编解码，再在特征上做SpecAugment频时掩码。每段平均经2.1个波形变换，93.5%至少经一个变换，裁剪上一半训练段被裁，一半裁到0.25到3秒，集中短语音。课程解决近亲混淆：17个2.5万步子阶段中，第一子阶段用正常温度配比，之后15个印欧雅利安语权重从0.45渐升到1.0，相当于先看大区分再看难区分。优化上峰值学习率取3×10的负4次方，5%热身加余弦衰减，42.5万步、每步144条，bf16加0.9999的指数滑动平均，在6张RTX A6000上约69.6小时。

[[CONCEPT_BRIDGE_4]]

下面这张图说明温度为何是头部换尾部的政策选择而非越大越好，横轴从自然分布走向均匀，纵轴左为跨语料性能、右为分资源层域内性能。

[[FIGURE_5]]

左图在T约2处见顶后回落，右图低资源线随T陡升、高资源线轻微下滑，域内无克什米尔等三语故最低层只含多格里和孔卡尼。论文据此停在2附近，并在全量取1.75配合下限，既保尾部又不让头部重复过拟合。

sections.heading: SUITE-102与SUITE-42如何保证测到真泛化
sections.body:
SUITE-102共102个条件、318,861条， headline 是IndicVoices每语言300条、共1,308个训练未见说话人的23类测试；跨语料层用FLEURS、SPRING-INX、MUCS、Kathbath、Common Voice的评测切分，与训练在片段级无交集；另有方言印地语、Hinglish、Svarah印度口音英语、录音室、讲座、乡村电话等变体探针。每个源再展开为0.25到10秒随机与VAD裁剪、0和5dB噪声、混响、G.711电话、babble、易混簇和开集试炼，开集用音乐、8种非印度语言和标签外的恰蒂斯加尔语。套件在最终训练前冻结。

SUITE-42是为昂贵API抽的子面板：37个核心条件覆盖10个所有系统都支持的语言，每语言每条件至多150条、共47,730条，加上5个全23类IndicVoices条件共17,229条，所有系统听完全相同的音频。提示类API被告知10或23候选，Sarvam自动检测，开放模型用原生标签集，Anuvani-LID始终在23类上预测，因此它可能犯10候选系统不可能犯的错误，另有一行限制到同样10候选的matched分数。主指标是条件内出现语言上的macro-F1，另报准确率、Cavg、等错误率、15箱期望校准误差和最大softmax的开集AUROC，区间用1,000次bootstrap，配对用McNemar加Holm或Bonferroni校正。

sections.heading: 37个核心条件上的总体排名是什么
sections.body:
核心问题是同 clip、跨域平均下专用模型是否仍领先通用大模型。比较条件是37个核心条件、每系统相同音频，指标方向macro-F1越高越好，Anuvani-LID在23类全空间打分，API在10候选中选。结果是Anuvani-LID均值0.914，Gemini 3.5 Flash 0.863，Sarvam 0.847，GPT-audio 0.735，最好的开放模型MMS-LID-126为0.826。配对差值均不含零，逐条件Anuvani-LID显著优于Gemini 21个、劣于9个，对每个开放模型至少28个条件显著更优。限制是商用API只给硬标签，无法比校准和Cavg，且版本会变。

下表整理核心均值与配对差距，差距指Anuvani-LID减去对方的百分点，区间为按条件分层的bootstrap 95%区间。

| 条件 | 指标 | Anuvani-LID | Gemini 3.5 Flash | 最佳开放模型 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 37核心条件 | 平均macro-F1 | 0.914 | 0.863 | 0.826 |
| 37核心条件 | 配对差距百分点 | — | 5.2 | 8.8 |
| 37核心条件 | 显著更好条件数 | — | 21 | 31 |

5.2点是23类全空间下的差距，限制到同样10候选时Anuvani-LID为0.923，领先扩大到6.0点，说明全空间打分并未占便宜。代价是仍有9个条件显著输给Gemini，集中在长朗读 clean 句，后文短语音表会显示优势完全反转。未胜出项是干净朗读和电话两域差距最小，仅1.9和1.8点。

[[CONCEPT_BRIDGE_5]]

校准上开发集拟合的单一温度0.674把全23测试的期望校准误差从0.054降到0.008，此时Cavg乘100为3.16、等错误率1.79%。开集上音乐和非印度语言AUROC达0.89到0.91，但近亲恰蒂斯加尔语只有0.84，说明拒识远亲易、拒识近亲难。

训练轨迹显示不同条件族不同时见顶，干净语音75k步见顶，电话175k，易混和开集200k，babble噪声混响短语音到425k才见顶，单取末检查点会丢掉早期信道鲁棒性。

[[FIGURE_8]]

左图虚线检查点与实点EMA随步数爬升但波动，右图7点平均达0.8453居31候选之首。相对末检查点，该汤把电话从0.898拉回0.923，babble噪声开集各涨0.4到0.6点，且无家族回退超0.5点，早期成员补回了后期侵蚀的信道能力。

sections.heading: 短语音、全23类与分领域差距有多大
sections.body:
第二个要回答的问题是优势从哪里来、短输入和全覆盖是否仍成立。按下表看，1秒FLEURS上Anuvani-LID为0.764，Gemini为0.520；域内1秒为0.854对0.611，都是24点差距；0.5秒为0.545对0.231，Sarvam为0.439。全23面板上Anuvani-LID平均0.897，Voxlect为0.713，Gemini为0.710，GPT-audio为0.384。21个语言F1超0.90，包括不足600小时的博多、多格里、桑塔利等，最低是印地语0.84和印度英语0.89。

| 条件 | 指标 | Anuvani-LID | Gemini 3.5 Flash | Sarvam/GPT-audio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FLEURS 1秒 | macro-F1 | 0.764 | 0.520 | 0.139 |
| 域内1秒 | macro-F1 | 0.854 | 0.611 | 0.767 |
| 全23面板 | 平均macro-F1 | 0.897 | 0.710 | 0.384 |
| FLEURS 0.5秒 | macro-F1 | 0.545 | 0.231 | 0.439 |
| 全23乌尔都语增益 | F1百分点 | 20.5 | — | — |

短语音是最大差距域，论文把原因归于时长裁剪增强，对手如Voxlect只在3到15秒上训练，从未见过短音频。分领域均值显示Anuvani-LID在9域中8域最优，对Gemini在短语音领先0.842对0.658，babble高7.0点，0dB噪声高6.0点，混响高4.3点。反例是Gemini在5个全长FLEURS切分和MUCS朗读上显著领先1.2到5.7点，维基式朗读句的词汇信息可被音频大模型利用；Hindi变体域也是对手领先，下一节结合混淆解释。

下图按领域展示均值，可见短、babble、噪声列差距最大，干净朗读差距最小。

[[FIGURE_9]]

图中Anuvani-LID行在短语音、电话、噪声、混响、babble、易混等列加粗居首，仅Hindi varieties列Sarvam更高。注意Anuvani-LID始终在23类上打分，API只在10候选中选，因此该差距是在更难的输出空间下取得的。

sections.heading: 池化损失与数据增强各自带来什么
sections.body:
消融要回答哪个组件决定精度、哪个决定校准、每种增强是否只动它模拟的轴。第一阶段25臂显示池化差异约1个百分点，损失决定校准：注意力池化加焦点损失跨语料0.840、期望校准误差0.023，而角间隔损失校准误差0.75以上；ECAPA加焦点为0.835，多2,300万参数仍未超0.840。编码器必须微调，冻结只有0.362，微调顶6层0.806，适配器和LoRA约0.82，全量微调领先48点。

| 对照轴 | 指标 | 注意力池化加焦点损失 | ECAPA加焦点损失 | 交叉熵对照 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 跨语料 | macro-F1 | 0.840 | 0.835 | 0.836 |
| 校准 | 原始期望校准误差 | 0.023 | 未更优 | 约0.06 |
| 参数 | 额外参数量 | — | 23M | — |

表前说明比较问题是同1,000小时、同4轮下头与损失的公平对照，指标方向macro-F1越高越好、误差越低越好。精度上焦点略高于交叉熵，但校准好2.6倍，且多格里召回从0.075提到0.20；ECAPA在ArcFace下发散、自蒸馏下过校正，多数投票也几乎拿不到oracle承诺的短语音11.1点增益，故保留单网络。负结果是层聚合top-1多对1.1%，才同时保留层混合。

增强的逐轴效果如下表，数值为相对无增强基线的macro-F1百分点变化，正为提升。

| 增强 | 0.5秒变化 | 1秒变化 | 噪声变化 | 干净代价 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 时长裁剪 | 9.5 | 6.4 | 1.3 | -0.3 |
| 噪声加混响 | -3.6 | 0.9 | 3.2 | -0.2 |
| 全栈四项 | 10.7 | 7.5 | 3.8 | -0.4 |
| 加babble | 0.2 | -0.8 | 0.0 | -0.2 |

每种扰动主要动它模拟的轴，时长裁剪管短语音，噪声加混响管噪声和混响，编解码管电话1.0点，SpecAugment小而均匀。单独噪声会伤0.5秒3.6点，但全栈组合后短语音仍涨10.7和7.5点，仅付干净语音0.4点代价。babble在全栈上再加9.5点babble域增益且干净不掉，证明多说话人babble不可被普通噪声替代。

下图用颜色展示上述行列对应关系，蓝为提升、橙为下降，黑框标出该行模拟的目标轴。

[[FIGURE_6]]

可见SpecAugment行全为浅蓝小增益，噪声行在噪声列深蓝但在0.5秒列深橙，时长裁剪行在短输入列深蓝，全栈行兼得各列而干净列仅浅橙0.4点，babble行只在babble列深蓝，支持各扰动各管一轴的结论。

sections.heading: 课程、采样与权重平均的取舍是什么
sections.body:
课程阶段在4,000小时、3轮下一次只动一轴。时长课程把裁剪从6.6秒经2.95秒缩到1.0秒，在5语料上0.5秒从0.42提到0.52、0.25秒从0.17提到0.26，但结尾全是短裁剪会伤长语音，因此最终用双峰裁剪保留长段。资源课程让温度从1.2升到2.0，方向反转则作对照；自步课程只让batch内最低损失68%参损，效果未超无课程。最终保留易混课程：15个印欧雅利安语权重从0.45升到1.0，因为三轮无课程 recipe 在全23测试的错误65%集中于此簇，且该簇是第二阶段最弱的干净轴0.909。

采样上单轮T=2跨语料0.919，两轮升到0.931，易混从0.885到0.909，退化音频从0.832到0.852。单独做再平衡时logit调整在T=1下与T=3的温度采样持平0.925且校准最优0.011，但叠在T=2上会数两遍先验，域内掉3.5点，英语从0.906掉到0.699，印地语从0.713掉到0.344，故只保留一个再平衡器。两阶段均匀加自然采样域内0.964高于单阶段两轮0.958，但开集从0.840掉到0.798，因此保留单阶段。权重平均上31候选中7点汤0.8453第一，相对末检查点电话和开集回升且无大家族回退超0.5点，期望校准误差也从0.077降到0.054。

sections.heading: 误差沿什么语言学结构分布
sections.body:
在说话人 disjoint 的全23测试6,900条上，61%错误留在参考语言的语系内，73%源于印欧雅利安语。最大混淆是亲缘对：印地语到迈蒂利语4.7%、反向2.0%，乌尔都语到印地语4.0%，多格里到印地语和旁遮普语，孔卡尼语到马拉地语2.3%，奥里亚语到阿萨姆语3.3%和到迈蒂利语2.3%。印地语因标签合并56种母语而最难，F1仅0.84。跨系错误多在东北长期接触区，如阿萨姆语到博多语3.0%、曼尼普尔语到博多语2.7%，地域相似在系谱树上不可见，录音地域重叠也可能贡献。

英语主要错向印地语2.7%、桑塔利语2.0%、马拉地语1.7%，符合母语影响元音、颤音和重音的报道；在覆盖19种母语的Svarah上40%英语被归到表定语言且分散多类。Hindi变体上19%方言印地语被标乌尔都语，Hinglish 28%到乌尔都语、23%到英语，口语印地语与乌尔都语共享一形，选择更多是社会语言学而非声学问题。matched下HiACC从0.551升到0.729，说明单标签打分在混合和方言上天然惩罚声学模型，帧级语种分割才是合适形式。

sections.heading: 语言信息在网络哪层与覆盖边界
sections.body:
线性探测显示预训练编码器语言峰在9到11块约0.56，到17块塌到0.13；1,000小时微调峰移到11块0.69，54.6k小时移到12块0.86，高于文献中自监督Conformer的低层最优。聚合权重给17块30%，其余多在10到16块，无单块敲除代价超0.08，而只用末块的模型绕过第7块会掉0.34，说明聚合买了鲁棒性。语料身份在顶层仍可线性解码0.90，但用LEACE擦除其三秩子空间后语种macro-F1只变0.1点，说明决策不靠信道捷径。截断到前12块以84M参数达0.848，超全17块116M的0.840，12块已够。

覆盖上标签只含22表定加印度英语，Bhili、Gondi、Tulu、博杰普尔等不在内，开集对近亲恰蒂斯加尔语AUROC仅0.84，远低于音乐和非印度语言的0.89到0.91。评测上Kathbath与训练共享456人中4人，只作域内对照；商用API行为随版本变，论文给出2026年7月16到21日的快照标识。阶段一到五每臂单次运行，小差异仍暂定；全量只训一次，虽有轨迹和未选中检查点0.912核心、0.889全23的核查表明排名不靠挑选，但未重复多种子。0.25秒7条件中7个仅0.24到0.35，无开放模型超0.18，次秒仍信息受限。

sections.heading: 复现第一步做什么与关键超参数
sections.body:
先按论文顺序重建评测再调模型。复现第一步是冻结SUITE式多轴切分：准备说话人 disjoint 的IndicVoices 23类测试、FLEURS等语料的评测切分并做片段级去交集，再展开0.25到10秒裁剪、噪声、混响、电话、babble和开集三条件，用macro-F1作主指标，bootstrap给区间。模型从公开MahaDhwani Conformer-L出发，接可学习层混合、注意力统计池化、256维嵌入和23路分类器，全量微调而非只训头。

关键超参数按原文：80维对数Mel、4倍下采样；焦点损失gamma取2、标签平滑0.1；采样T取1.75、英语下限16%、印地语下限11%、17子阶段易混课程从0.45到1.0；一半训练段裁剪、其中一半对数均匀在0.25到3秒；变速0.95到1.05概率0.5、噪声0到15dB概率0.5、混响概率0.3、编解码概率0.3、babble概率0.2；AdamW峰值3×10的负4次方、5%热身余弦到10的负6次方、42.5万步每步144条、EMA 0.9999；推理温度0.674。作者资源在Hugging Face的CIIL/Anuvani-LID链接本次未能确认可达，第三方托管不能当作作者已开源的证据，开源、权重可下载、可运行需分开核实。还需补性别分片、更多种子和帧级混合评测。

sections.heading: 什么时候值得尝试与还缺哪项验证
sections.body:
当管线首步要在印度语言上做路由或拒识，且音频短、噪声大、含电话窄带，或必须输出可信置信度时，值得尝试这种专用小模型：它在1秒和全23覆盖上领先最大，且115M量级远小于Whisper-large-v3的1.55B，校准后期望误差可到0.008。当输入全是长朗读 clean 句且可利用词汇信息，或只需区分10个大语种、不需尾部小语种时，通用音频大模型可能已够，论文中Gemini在全长FLEURS和MUCS上反而领先。

容易产生的误解是把干净域内98%左右的饱和精度当成已解决，论文 pilot 显示所有头都在98%上下1点内，换到跨语料多轴才拉开差距；也不能把搜索选出的汤增益或oracle融合上限当成部署可得，汤是参数平均无推理代价但仍需在held-out上选成员，oracle多数投票几乎拿不到11.1点。仍缺的验证是跨种子全量重复、性别分片性能、乡村电话外的新信道，以及对表定外近亲的系统性拒识和Hinglish帧级分割。下一步应把单标签分类扩展为语码混合的帧级划分，同时补上延迟与成本实测，再谈部署收益。

cases.sourceText:
Anuvani-LID: Robust and Calibrated Spoken Language Identification
for Indian Languages
Stephen Fernandes
Affiliation: Central Institute of Indian Languages
Narayan Choudhary
Affiliation: stephenn.fernandes@gmail.com, n.choudhary@gov.in
Abstract
Every multilingual speech pipeline begins with a language decision, an error there propagates silently through recognition, translation and routing. In India it spans 22 scheduled languages across four language families, heard over short, noisy, narrowband and code-mixed audio. Foundational speech models increasingly present language identification (LID) as an inherent latent, generalized capability. Autoregressive decoders in speech models emit a special language ID token, and modern LLMs with audio capabilities can name the language when prompted. We test this assumption on identical clips and find that whisper and similar speech models has tokens for only 15 of the 23 languages, on one second inputs Gemini 3.5 Flash reaches 0.52 macro-F1 and GPT-audio 0.14. We present Anuvani LID, a dedicated 115M parameter LID conformer model trained on 54,643 hours of Indian speech spanning 22 Indian languages and Indian accented English. Along with designed and controlled studies on 102 condition benchmark with speaker and corpus held out tests. Across 37 conditions, it reaches 0.914 mean macro-F1, 5.2 points above Gemini 3.5 Flash and ahead of 14 other systems. It is 24 points ahead of Gemini at one second, scores 0.897 on all 23 languages where no other system exceeds 0.713, and is calibrated to an ECE of 0.008. Reliable Indian LID still requires a robust, dedicated and calibrated model.11
 1
 The released model is available at: https://huggingface.co/CIIL/Anuvani-LID.
Figure 1: Anuvani-LID against the field on SUITE-42 (macro-F1, identical clips). The radar covers nine domains from 32 of the 37 core conditions, with its axis from 0.3; the leaderboard averages all 37; the bars show the four domains with the largest margin. The prompted APIs chose among 10 candidate languages, Anuvani-LID among all 23.
1 Introduction
Spoken language identification (LID) is the first decision in almost every multilingual speech pipeline: it chooses the recogniser, the translation direction and the language a helpline or assistant answers in (Li et al., 2013). An error here propagates; a Maithili call sent to a Hindi recogniser degrades every later component. In India this decision is usually hard and complex. The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages from four language families, the mother tongues of 96.7% of the 1.21 billion people counted in 2011 (ORGI, 2018). Many are close relatives, our training audio ranges from 13,039 h (Indian accented English) to 369 h (Kashmiri) in our pool, and deployed audio is short, noisy, narrowband and code-mixed (§2).
Speech foundational models represent LID task as a latent, in-context generalised capability. Whisper decoder decodes a language ID token before it transcribes (Radford et al., 2023), Meta’s MMS models attaches a 4,017 language identification head (Pratap et al., 2024), and LLMs with audio capabilities such as Gemini and GPT-audio name the language of a clip when asked (Google DeepMind, 2026; OpenAI, 2024). Dedicated LID models might therefore seem obsolete. For Indian languages, our measurements argue otherwise (§6):
• 
Coverage is incomplete. Whisper has tokens for only 15 of the 23 classes (22 scheduled languages plus English), and among open systems only Voxlect covers all 23.
• 
Short inputs break generalist systems. At one second audio length, Gemini 3.5 Flash reaches 0.52 macro-F1 and GPT-audio 0.14. At sub one second, most speech models fail.
• 
Errors matter even at foundation-model scale. Most of Whisper’s supposed Welsh translation data turned out to be English audio misclassified by its language identifier (Radford et al., 2023). Even at the scale of Gemini 3.5 Flash, errors matter.
• 
Deployment needs calibrated scores and small models. Routing and rejection need calibrated confidence, which hard-label APIs often lack, and Whisper-large-v3 has 1.55B parameters (OpenAI, 2023), 13 times more than Anuvani-LID.
A further obstacle is methodological. Clean, in-domain test sets saturate: in our pilot study every head reached about 98% macro-averaged accuracy, within 1 pp of the others. Following work on saturation and shortcut learning (Geirhos et al., 2020; Kiela et al., 2021), we rebuilt the evaluation pipeline first and took every later decision on held-out, multi-axis conditions. We report the programme in the order it was carried out. Our contributions are:
• 
SUITE-102, a 102-condition, 318,861-utterance benchmark with speaker- and corpus-held-out tiers, and SUITE-42, which scores 15 open and commercial systems on identical clips (§4).
• 
A staged, controlled study of fine-tuning a self-supervised Conformer for LID (§5).
• 
Anuvani-LID, which leads all 15 systems (Figure 1), most clearly on short, noisy and all-23-language conditions, and is well calibrated (§6).
• 
A linguistic error analysis (§7) and a layer analysis showing that 12 of 17 blocks suffice (§8).

Figure 2: Speaker population versus training data. Speech resources do not track population: Urdu has more than 50M first-language speakers but less audio than Maithili or Nepali, and English is abundant because most of its 128.5M speakers use it as a second or third language. The diagonals mark 10, 100 and 1,000 training hours per million speakers.
Twenty-two languages by design.
The Eighth Schedule for Indian languages grew from 14 to 22 languages through additions in 1967, 1992 and 2004 (Government of India, 2026; MHA, 2017). The 2011 Census rationalised 19,569 raw mother-tongue returns into 1,369 mother tongues and 121 languages (ORGI, 2018). Speaker numbers span four orders of magnitude, from Hindi (528M) to Sanskrit (24,821), and training data does not track them (Table 1; Figure 2). The labels are administrative: the Census “Hindi” groups 56 mother tongues, including Bhojpuri (50.6M), and Maithili was counted under Hindi until 2001 (ORGI, 2018), so class boundaries are partly conventional (MHA, 2017).
Four families, one linguistic area.
Fifteen scheduled languages are Indo-Aryan, four Dravidian, two Tibeto-Burman and one Austroasiatic (Hammarström et al., 2026). Genealogy understates how alike they sound. Emeneau (1956) described India as a linguistic area in which languages of all families share retroflex consonants, verb-final clauses and echo words (Masica, 1976), and retroflex systems are distributed geographically rather than genetically (Arsenault, 2017). Indian LID work reports heavily overlapping phone sets (Vuddagiri et al., 2018; Dey et al., 2022), and on FLEURS the South Asian group has the lowest LID accuracy (Conneau et al., 2023). Several classes are sisters or former dialects. Hindi and Urdu share colloquial Hindustani (Kachru, 2008), and Urdu→\toHindi is VoxLingua107’s most common error (Valk and Alumäe, 2021). Grierson treated Dogri as a dialect of Punjabi and Konkani as one of Marathi (Grierson, 1916; Grierson, 1905), and these pairs share 93% and 80–82% of basic vocabulary (Kogan, 2016). Script, which separates Hindi from Urdu (“one language, two scripts”; King, 1994), is absent from speech. The remaining evidence is sparse in short clips: degree of retroflexion, laryngeal contrasts, vowel length, and lexical tone in Punjabi, Dogri, Bodo and Meitei.
Close relatives and dialect continua.
Several scheduled languages are sisters or former “dialects” of one another:
• 
Hindi and Urdu are sister languoids under Hindustani and share a colloquial form (Hammarström et al., 2026; Kachru, 2008). Urdu→\toHindi is the single most common error in VoxLingua107 (Valk and Alumäe, 2021).
• 
Punjabi and Dogri share 93% of basic vocabulary (Kogan, 2016), and Grierson (1916) described Dogri as a dialect of Punjabi.
• 
Grierson (1905) likewise treated Konkani as a Marathi dialect; the two share 80–82% of basic vocabulary.
• 
Assamese, Bengali and Odia share 86–88% of basic vocabulary and one Glottolog node, and they share numeral-classifier morphology with Maithili (Emeneau, 1956).
• 
Maithili speakers from the eastern dialect area commonly shift to Hindi when talking with speakers from other areas (Central Institute of Indian Languages, n.d.).
Lexicostatistics measures vocabulary, not acoustics, but these are exactly the pairs where LID systems err (§7).
What the signal carries.
Script is absent from speech. Devanagari alone serves at least ten of the classes (Unicode Consortium, 2026). Hindi and Urdu, famously “one language, two scripts” (King, 1994), are written in Devanagari and Perso-Arabic respectively. Labels must therefore come from corpus metadata rather than from transcripts. The discriminative evidence is phonetic, phonotactic and prosodic:
• 
Degree of retroflexion: Tamil exceeds Hindi, and Nepali retroflexes are weaker still (Keane, 2004; Khatiwada, 2009).
• 
Laryngeal series: Hindi has a four-way stop series (Ohala, 1994), and Gujarati contrasts breathy and modal voice on vowels (Esposito and Khan, 2012).
• 
Vowel length: contrastive in Dravidian languages but not in Bengali or Assamese (Keane, 2004; Khan, 2010; Mahanta, 2012).
• 
Lexical tone: documented in Punjabi and Dogri and in Bodo and Meitei (Evans et al., 2018; Das and Mahanta, 2019; Devi and Das, 2024).
• 
Rare segments: Sindhi implosives and Santali checked finals (Maddieson, 2013; The Unicode Consortium, 2025).
Many of these cues are sparse, and a one-second clip may contain none of them. This is consistent with duration, rather than noise, being the dominant difficulty axis (§6).
Indian English, not English.
The 23rd class is Indian accented English. Every English hour in our pool comes from Indian speakers, consisting of NPTEL lectures (10,441 h), NLTM collections (1,252 h), ULCA (916 h) and Indic TIMIT (234 h; Yarra et al., 2019), and we evaluate on Indian-accented sets such as Svarah (Javed et al., 2023b). Kachru (1986) called Indian English “an Indian language in its own right”; 128.5M Indians speak it, nearly all as a second or third language (ORGI, 2011). Its accent is at once uniform and variable (Wiltshire, 2020; Sailaja, 2009; Pandey, 2015). Pan-Indian features include apical, often retroflex /t d/, stops for /T D/, merged /v/–/w/ and unaspirated voiceless stops (Masica, 1972), and a rhythm that differs from British English in duration, loudness, pitch and glottal stops (Fuchs, 2016). Beneath them, the mother tongue shapes vowels, rhotics, diphthongs and pitch accents (Wiltshire and Harnsberger, 2006; Maxwell and Fletcher, 2010). Svarah’s 117 speakers from 65 districts cover 19 first languages, and Whisper’s word error rate rises from 2.7% on LibriSpeech to 7.2% on it (Javed et al., 2023b). For LID this cuts both ways. The English class must absorb all this variation, and each English utterance carries traces of the very languages the model must also recognise (§7).
Multilingual speakers.
In 2011, 26.0% of Indians reported a second language and 7.1% a third (ORGI, 2022). About 17% of Hindi–English social-media posts are code-mixed (Bali et al., 2014). In code-switched speech, more than half of the embedded segments last only 200–400 ms (Barras et al., 2020), so the matrix language is the natural utterance label.
3 Related Work
Spoken LID.
LID moved from i-vectors (Li et al., 2013) to x-vectors (Snyder et al., 2018b; Snyder et al., 2018a) and ECAPA-TDNN (Desplanques et al., 2020), with VoxLingua107 (Valk and Alumäe, 2021) behind common open baselines (SpeechBrain, 2021; Jia et al., 2023). Self-supervised (SSL) speech encoders now dominate the space with XLS-R and MMS type models as well as dedicate finetune’s wav2vec 2.0-style models exists (Babu et al., 2022; Pratap et al., 2024; Baevski et al., 2020), and Bartley et al. (2023) fine-tune an SSL Conformer. NIST LRE defines cluster-aware evaluation with CavgC_{\text{avg}} (Sadjadi et al., 2018; NIST, 2022).
Indian-language LID.
IIITH-ILSC (Vuddagiri et al., 2018) introduced a 23-class benchmark. Later systems added CTC features (Mandava et al., 2019) or fine-tuned XLSR-53 (Gupta et al., 2023; Rajak et al., 2025). Cross-corpus generalisation is the central difficulty for such models: EER rises from 11.8% in-corpus to 43.3% cross-corpus (Dey et al., 2021), and acoustic augmentation and bias compensation recovers only part of it (Dey et al., 2023; Dey et al., 2024). Surveys and layer studies include Dey et al. (2022) and Dey and Saha (2025). On IndicSUPERB, 12-language LID accuracy falls from 98.2% on seen to 90.8% on unseen speakers (Javed et al., 2023a), and Basu et al. (2026) compare encoders for 42 Indic languages. We differ in scale (54.6k h), converging all 23 spoken language classes, held-out multi-axis evaluation, and comparison with commercial audio LLMs. We build upon the MahaDhwani encoder, which was pretrained w2v-BERT-style on 279k h of Indian audio (Bhogale et al., 2025; Chung et al., 2021).
4 SUITE-102: A De-saturated Benchmark
Design.
SUITE-102 probes LID along the multi-domain axes on which deployed systems fail (composition in Appendix Table 4). Its headline tier is the IndicVoices test set (Javed et al., 2024a): 300 spontaneous utterances per language for all 23 classes, from 1,308 speakers, none of whom is among the 34,034 IndicVoices speakers in our training data. Cross-corpus tiers use the evaluation splits of FLEURS, SPRING-INX, MUCS, Kathbath and Common Voice (Conneau et al., 2023; Nithya R et al., 2023; Diwan et al., 2021; Javed et al., 2023a; Ardila et al., 2020). The clip-level carve has an empty intersection with training, and transcript fingerprinting finds no FLEURS or MUCS overlap. Variety probes cover dialectal Hindi (Javed et al., 2024b), Hinglish (Singh et al., 2025), Indian-accented English (Javed et al., 2023b), studio speech (Baby et al., 2016), lectures (AI4Bharat, 2020) and rural telephony (Bhanushali et al., 2022). Each source is expanded into random and VAD-anchored crops of 0.25–10 s, MUSAN noise at 0 and 5 dB (Snyder et al., 2015), reverberation (Ko et al., 2017), G.711 μ\mu-law telephony, babble, confusable-cluster subsets and open-set trials. The open-set trials use music, eight non-Indian languages and Chhattisgarhi, a relative of Hindi outside the label set. Curation is deterministic, and the suite was frozen before the final training run.
SUITE-42.
Commercial APIs are too costly to run on the full suite, so we drew a balanced panel of 42 conditions with up to 150 utterances per language in each. The core panel has 37 conditions (47,730 clips) over the ten languages every system supports: Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Punjabi and Urdu. The all-23 panel has five IndicVoices conditions (17,229 clips). Every system receives identical audio. Prompted audio LLMs and Azure receive the candidate list (10 or 23 languages), Sarvam Saaras runs in auto-detect mode, and open models predict over their native label sets. Anuvani-LID always predicts over all 23 classes, so it can make errors that a 10-candidate system cannot. We also report it restricted to the same ten candidates (“matched”).
Metrics and statistics.
The primary metric is macro-F1 over the languages present in a condition. We also report top-1 accuracy, CavgC_{\text{avg}} (NIST, 2022), EER, 15-bin ECE (Pakdaman Naeini et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017), and open-set AUROC from maximum softmax probability (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017). Intervals are 1,000-resample bootstraps (Bisani and Ney, 2004) (300, stratified by condition, for paired differences), and paired items are tested with McNemar’s test (McNemar, 1947; Gillick and Cox, 1989) under Holm or Bonferroni correction (Holm, 1979).

Anuvani-LID fine-tunes the released MahaDhwani Conformer-L encoder (Bhogale et al., 2025; AI4Bharat, 2024), which was pretrained self-supervised on 279k h of large scale raw Indian audio (Figure 3). The head mixes all block outputs with learned weights, 𝐳t=∑ℓαℓ​𝐡ℓ,t\mathbf{z}_{t}=\sum_{\ell}\alpha_{\ell}\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t} with 𝜶=softmax⁡(𝐰)\bm{\alpha}=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{w}) (Yang et al., 2021). It then applies attentive statistics pooling (Okabe et al., 2018), a 256-dimensional embedding and a 23-way classifier (115.6M parameters in total). 5.2 A staged research programme
The recipe is the outcome of six stages run in order, each starting from the previous stage’s promoted recipe (Appendix Table 5). Stages I–V ran at reduced scale (1,000–4,000 h) so that many controlled arms were affordable; Stage VI trained once on all 54,643 h, so that recipes here onwards could be validated on the full scale of training data.
Each stage answers one question with arms that change one axis at a time against the recipe it inherits, and architecture, sampling and augmentation are judged on held-out conditions (§4) rather than on in-domain validation accuracy, which saturates.

Stage I: head, loss and adaptation search at 1,000 h.
The first decision was the optimiser, because the heads under comparison differ in trainable size by two orders of magnitude, from LoRA adapters to an ECAPA-TDNN fine-tuned end to end. ULMFiT-style discriminative rates (Howard and Ruder, 2018), a larger step for the freshly initialised head than for the pre-trained encoder, are the usual prescription for this setting. We tested them against a single global rate on three heads that span the range, attentive pooling, NetVLAD and ECAPA-TDNN, for 1,500 steps each. A head rate ten times the encoder’s (10−310^{-3} against 10−410^{-4}) gave the large NetVLAD head nothing (0.980 against 0.982 macro-averaged validation accuracy) and destabilised the angular-margin attentive head, so a single global rate of 10−410^{-4}, at which the pre-trained encoder and the new head co-adapt stably, became the default for every fully fine-tuned arm.
We trained 25 arms on a balanced 1,000 h subset of 20 languages (Kashmiri, Santali and Sindhi had too little audio) and scored them on the 54-condition predecessor of SUITE-102 (Figure 4). Every arm shared one recipe apart from the axis under test: AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with β=(0.9,0.98)\beta{=}(0.9,0.98) and weight decay 10−310^{-3}, 10% linear warm-up and cosine decay to 10−610^{-6}, 144 utterances per step, temperature sampling at T=2T{=}2, bf16 and four epochs.
Three findings shaped the model:
• 
Pooling matters little. Under an additive angular margin (AAM) loss, statistics (Snyder et al., 2018b), multi-head (India et al., 2019), NetVLAD (Arandjelović et al., 2016), ECAPA-TDNN (Desplanques et al., 2020) and attentive pooling over aggregated layers all land within 0.825–0.837 cross-corpus macro-F1, with overlapping intervals.
• 
The loss decides calibration. Cosine-margin heads (Deng et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018) emit bounded, rescaled cosines, and fine-tuned cosine-margin heads have an ECE of 0.75–0.79; softmax heads reach 0.02–0.08 (0.13 under distillation). With attentive pooling, focal loss has the highest macro-F1 of all 25 arms (0.840) and an ECE of 0.023, 2.6×\times below cross-entropy, in line with Mukhoti et al. (2020); layer aggregation, however, classifies 1.1% more items correctly on top-1, so we kept both.
• 
The encoder must be fine-tuned. A frozen encoder reaches only 0.362, and top-6 fine-tuning (0.806), adapters (0.822; Houlsby et al., 2019) and LoRA (0.821; Hu et al., 2022) all trail full fine-tuning. These partial regimes ran at the larger rates prescribed for small trainable budgets, 10−310^{-3} for the frozen encoder’s head, for bottleneck adapters of width 64 and for LoRA of rank 8 (α=16\alpha{=}16), and 3×10−43{\times}10^{-4} for the top six blocks, and the frozen encoder trails full fine-tuning by 48 points.
ECAPA-TDNN (Desplanques et al., 2020), explored in 12 arms, was set aside: its deep head drives the arccos-based ArcFace to divergence, it over-corrects under focal loss and under self-distillation (Hinton et al., 2015), and no ECAPA arm passes attentive pooling with focal loss on cross-corpus macro-F1 (0.835 against 0.840) despite 23M extra parameters. Fusing arms promises up to 11.1 points on short utterances under an oracle, but majority vote recovers almost none of it, so we kept a single network, the simplest arm at the top of the cross-corpus ranking: attentive statistics pooling, focal loss and full fine-tuning.

Each perturbation mainly improves the axis it simulates (Figure 6):
• 
random duration cropping: +9.5 pp at 0.5 s and +6.4 pp at 1 s;
• 
MUSAN noise with room impulse responses: +3.2 pp in noise and +1.6 pp in reverberation and babble (alone it costs 3.6 pp at 0.5 s);
• 
μ\mu-law/8 kHz codec simulation: +1.0 pp on telephony;
• 
SpecAugment: small, uniform gains;
• 
multi-talker babble, 1–6 overlapping talkers at 5–18 dB SNR, on top of the other four: +11.6 pp on the seven babble conditions (0.804 to 0.920 macro-F1), with no cost on clean conditions (+0.3 pp).
Combined, the other four gain 10.7 pp at 0.5 s, 7.5 at 1 s, 3.8 in noise, 2.0 in reverberation and babble, and 1.2 on telephony, for a 0.4 pp cost on clean speech. The final recipe crops half of the training segments. Half of those crops are drawn log-uniformly between 0.25 and 3 s and the rest uniformly between 3 and 16 s, which concentrates training mass on the short durations that interactive systems receive.
Eight operations make up the final recipe (Table 2). Six act on the waveform as each clip leaves the data loader, always in the same order: speed perturbation (Ko et al., 2015), additive noise from MUSAN (Snyder et al., 2015), reverberation with simulated room impulse responses (Ko et al., 2017), the duration crop, babble and the codec. Noise therefore enters before the room response and is reverberated with the speech, babble is mixed in at the cropped length, and the telephone channel acts last, on the whole mixture, as it does in a call. The other two are the frequency and time masks of SpecAugment (Park et al., 2019), applied to the log-Mel features of every training example. Each waveform transform is selected independently for every clip, with a fixed probability that depends on neither the language nor the corpus, so no transform can become a cue for a class, and its parameters are drawn afresh each time. The six selections give 64 combinations. Over the 61.2M training examples of the final run, 102.5k h of source audio, 93.5% pass through at least one waveform transform and 6.5% reach the masks unaltered. A clip receives 2.1 waveform transforms on average, and 70.3% receive two or more. Speed perturbation picks one of five rates from 0.95 to 1.05 and leaves the clip as it is at the identity rate, so it changes 40% of clips. Half of the clips are selected for cropping, but a crop from the long branch, uniform between 3 s and the clip’s own length, cannot shorten a clip of 3 s or less, so 44.9% are shortened; a quarter of all examples, 15.3M, are cut to between 0.25 and 3 s. Noise comes from 930 MUSAN recordings, and reverberation from 60,000 impulse responses simulated in 600 rooms, 200 each small, medium and large. Babble sums one to six talkers drawn from 10,426 recordings: the 426 speech recordings of MUSAN, as in x-vector training (Snyder et al., 2018b), and 10,000 training clips spread over all 23 languages. The codec band-limits to 4 kHz by resampling through 8 kHz and applies 8-bit G.711 μ\mu-law companding (ITU-T, 1988). The Stage III arms used the same probabilities, with a single uniform crop of 0.5–16 s, and babble only in its own arm.

Stage IV: curriculum learning.
Stages I–III fix what the model sees; Stage IV asks whether the order in which it sees it adds more (Bengio et al., 2009). We expected the largest return where the static recipe left most error: on the confusable Indo-Aryan cluster, the weakest clean axis of Stage II (0.909 macro-F1 on confusable pairs), and on sub-second input. Following the decomposition of a curriculum into a difficulty measure and a training scheduler (Wang et al., 2022), we screened four definitions of difficulty under one competence schedule (Platanios et al., 2019), p⁡(e)=min⁡(1,e⁡(1−p02)/(N−1)+p02)p(e)=\min\bigl(1,\sqrt{e\,(1-p_{0}^{2})/(N-1)+p_{0}^{2}}\bigr) with p0=0.2p_{0}{=}0.2, which moves an axis from its easy end to its hard end over NN epochs. Each arm changed one axis of the Stage III recipe (4,000 h, three epochs) and had to lift its target without regressing any resource tier or language:
• 
Duration. Training crops shrink from 6.6 to 2.95 to 1.0 s, replacing the static random crop. This inverts SortaGrad (Amodei et al., 2016): a short clip is easy for recognition but carries less evidence for LID.
• 
Resource. The sampling temperature rises from 1.2 to 2.0, so the head dominates early and the tail gains weight late, after the annealed language sampling of mmBERT (Marone et al., 2025); a reverse schedule, from 1.8 to 1.0, controls for direction.
• 
Confusability. The 15 Indo-Aryan languages enter at 0.36 of their temperature-sampled weight, rising to 0.78 and then 1.0, so the Dravidian, Tibeto-Burman and Austroasiatic languages and English are seen at full weight first and the cluster in which most confusions arise (§7) is brought in gradually.
• 
Self-paced. Within each batch only the lowest-loss 68% of examples enter the loss, rising to all of them (Kumar et al., 2010).
Ordering by duration gives the largest short-input gain of any curriculum. Against the unscheduled recipe trained for the same three epochs, it lifts mean macro-F1 over five corpora from 0.42–0.43 to 0.52 at 0.5 s and from 0.17–0.18 to 0.26 at 0.25 s. Because ending training on one-second crops also shortens what the model hears of full-length speech, the final recipe takes the same short-crop exposure from the bimodal crop of Stage III, which keeps long segments in every batch. The model-driven gate did not add to the unscheduled recipe.

The final recipe schedules the language mix. It keeps the confusability curriculum, which acts on the cluster that carries most errors, composes with temperature sampling by changing which languages fill a batch as training proceeds rather than how often each is drawn relative to its size, and costs nothing at inference. At full scale its competence ramp spans the 17 sub-epochs of 25k steps that make up the 425k-step budget: after a first sub-epoch on the plain temperature mix, the weight of the Indo-Aryan cluster rises from 0.45 to 1.0 (Figure 7), on top of T=1.75T{=}1.75 and the language floors of Stage V. The schedule is applied in the streaming shard reader exactly as in the reference sampler (the language distributions agree to 10−1310^{-13}), and the final run logs it at every sub-epoch. We chose this curriculum on the evidence of the ablations. Confusable pairs were the weakest clean axis of Stage II (0.909 macro-F1), and the Indo-Aryan cluster carries most of the remaining errors: 65–66% of those of the unscheduled three-epoch recipe on the all-23 test. Each of the other three curricula either acts elsewhere or would move a tuned setting. The bimodal crop of Stage III already supplies the short-crop exposure of the duration curriculum while keeping long segments in every batch, the model-driven gate did not add to the unscheduled recipe, and the resource curriculum keeps the sampling temperature away from T=2T{=}2, where the inverted U of Stage II peaks, for most of training. The confusability curriculum alone targets the dominant error while keeping temperature sampling and the language floors as tuned, and it returns to the tuned mix by the last sub-epoch.
Stage V: scale-aware optimisation.
Short probes on the 4,000 h proxy set the optimiser. This proxy was redrawn from the final 54,643 h pool with the Stage II construction, so its language ratios match the full pool. Learning rates of 3×10−53{\times}10^{-5} to 10−310^{-3} gave development accuracies of 0.771–0.876; we took the knee at 3×10−43{\times}10^{-4}, since the last step added only 0.5 pp. Short horizons flatter large rates, so we checked the choice at length: at 3×10−43{\times}10^{-4} development accuracy reached 0.941 after 25k steps, a level the earlier 10−410^{-4} recipe needed about 46k steps to reach. Warm-ups of 5–15% and temperatures of 1.5–2.5 were flat within 1.2 pp, so we chose T=1.75T{=}1.75 with floors keeping English at 16% and Hindi at 11% of samples. T=1.75T{=}1.75 is the value at which the full augmentation stack, babble included, was validated, and because the proxy keeps the pool’s language ratios, the same temperature yields the same sampling mix at full scale; only the number of repetitions grows. The floors protect the two largest classes. Temperature sampling alone would give English 12.3% and Hindi 10.6% of draws, and under focal loss, which discounts easy examples, that leaves the head too little exposure; the Hindi floor also guards the Hindi–Urdu boundary. We sized the budget by effective passes: over 425k steps of 144 utterances, the five lowest-resource languages are seen four to six times each and the high-resource languages 1.3 to 2.2 times. With the tail replayed several times, label smoothing of 0.1 (Szegedy et al., 2016) guards against memorisation. To feed this budget, a sequential shard reader streams the corpus from a columnar store: it cuts read amplification from 38×\times to 0.97×\times and delivers 449 clips/s per data worker against a training demand of about 180, so the GPUs, not the disks, set the pace.

Stage VI: full-scale training and weight averaging.
The final run trains on all 54,643 h (31.24M utterances) for 425k steps with AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019), cosine decay, the confusability curriculum of Stage IV, bf16 and an EMA of the weights with decay 0.9999, on six RTX A6000 GPUs (Appendix B). It took 69.6 h, and development accuracy rose to 0.951 at the final checkpoint. SUITE-102 macro-F1 climbs from 0.782 at 25k steps to 0.844 for the final EMA weights (Figure 8), but the condition families do not peak together. Clean speech peaks at 75k steps, telephony at 175k, confusable pairs and open-set rejection at 200k, and babble, noise, reverberation and short utterances only at 425k. A single late checkpoint therefore keeps the optima reached at the end of training and gives up the earlier ones. Telephony, for instance, falls from 0.932 at its peak to 0.898 at the final step, and the EMA, with a horizon of about 10k steps, averages only the end of the run. We therefore finalise the model as recent large-scale training recipes do, by averaging weights along the training trajectory (Izmailov et al., 2018; Wortsman et al., 2022). Llama 3 averages checkpoints from its annealing phase (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and OLMo 2 averages independently annealed runs (Team OLMo et al., 2024). We archived a checkpoint every 25k steps beside its EMA shadow and scored 31 candidates on all 102 conditions: the 17 checkpoints, six late EMA shadows, five averages over contiguous or diverse subsets, and three soups whose members were fixed from the per-family profiles before any soup was scored. Every average is uniform over parameters and normalisation statistics, accumulated in float64. The best candidate, a soup of seven checkpoints at 100k, 175k, 275k, 325k, 350k, 400k and 425k steps, scores 0.8453 and is the released Anuvani-LID. Against the final checkpoint, it lifts telephony from 0.898 to 0.923 and babble, noise and open-set rejection by 0.6, 0.4 and 0.4 points. It also lowers raw ECE on the all-23 test from 0.077 to 0.054, while no condition family falls by more than 0.5 points. Early members bring back the channel robustness that late training erodes. Because the average is taken in weight space, unlike the output-space fusion of Stage I, it costs nothing at inference.

Where the margin comes from.
Anuvani-LID has the best mean in eight of nine domains (Figure 9). Its margin over Gemini is largest on short utterances (0.842 against 0.658), babble (+7.0), noise at 0 dB (+6.0) and reverberation (+4.3), and smallest on clean read speech (+1.9) and telephony (+1.8). It holds cross-corpus on SPRING-INX (0.953 against 0.865). Gemini is significantly better on six long read-speech conditions, the five full-length FLEURS slices and MUCS, by 1.2–5.7 points (Appendix D); read sentences such as FLEURS’s Wikipedia text (Conneau et al., 2023) offer lexical content an audio LLM can exploit. It is also better on two Hindi-variety probes (§7).
Short utterances.
Duration separates systems most. At one second Anuvani-LID reaches 0.764 macro-F1 on FLEURS and 0.854 in-domain, 24 points above Gemini in both cases (0.520, 0.611). At 0.5 s it reaches 0.545, against 0.439 for Sarvam and 0.231 for Gemini. Duration cropping (Stage III) plausibly explains the gap; some competitors never saw short audio, and Voxlect, for example, was trained on 3–15 s clips (Feng, 2025).
